title: Policy synthesis: thresholds and fallthrough notes
content:
Summary

Working notes on synthesizing routing policies that trade latency, cost, and reliability using threshold-driven gates and explicit fallthroughs. This doc is intentionally tactical — sketches, heuristics, and a couple of concrete threshold proposals for the control-plane policy engine. Not a finished spec; aim is to capture a repeatable approach we can test in the staging canary.

Background / motivation

We already route across regions and model variants based on score functions (latency, cost, reliability) but the current heuristics are distributed across routers and ad-hoc failovers. Operators want a more auditable, deterministic policy that is:
- easy to reason about for on-call (simple thresholds + explicit fallbacks)
- parameterizable for customer SLAs (per-route overrides)
- compatible with autoscaling and capacity signals
- cheap to evaluate in the control plane (no heavy ML inference on policy path)

Goals for the synthesized policy primitive

1) Predictable behavior: identical inputs + policy = identical routing decision (given same runtime metrics snapshot).
2) Transparent fallthroughs: every "reject" must have a deterministic next-hop.
3) Cheap scoring: threshold checks and simple arithmetic only.
4) Configurable per-tenant or per-route overrides (SLO priority).
5) Observability hooks: labels + decision-reason emitted for tracing and billing.

High-level approach

Policy primitive = ordered list of rule blocks. Each block is a conjunction of predicate checks (latency, error-rate, capacity, cost) and an action (route to backend X, degrade to variant Y, or continue). Predicate checks evaluate against aggregated signals over short windows (p95 / p50 latency, 1m error rate, active-connections, available-GPU). Rules are evaluated top-to-bottom. First matching rule's action is executed. If action is "continue", evaluation proceeds to the next block (explicit fallthrough).

Key primitives

- latency_p95 < T_ms
- p50_latency < T2_ms (used for fast path preference)
- error_rate_1m < E_pct
- capacity_utilization < C_pct (available GPU memory / inference slots)
- cost_delta < D_usd_per_req (estimated incremental cost compared to baseline)
- sloa_priority >= N (tenant SLO priority number)
- zone_health == healthy / degraded / offline

Example rule block (pseudo-yaml in plain text):
- name: prefer-local-fast-variants
  predicates: [latency_p95 < 20, error_rate_1m < 0.4, capacity_utilization < 0.75]
  action: route: region-local-quantized-v2

- name: warm-fallback-quantized
  predicates: [latency_p95 < 60, error_rate_1m < 1.5, capacity_utilization < 0.9]
  action: route: nearest-quantized-v1

- name: cost-sensitive-steer
  predicates: [cost_delta < 0.001, sloa_priority < 3]
  action: route: low-cost-variant

- name: degrade-to-hosted
  predicates: [true]
  action: route: hosted-fallback (and emit reason)

Notes on thresholds and aggregation windows

- Use short windows for latency (20s-60s sliding) to maintain sensitivity; use longer windows (1m-5m) for error rates to avoid flapping on single transient spikes.
- Default thresholds should be conservative; let canaries exercise tightened thresholds.
- Provide two modes in control-plane configs: "strict" (tighter thresholds, less likely to use cheap/backstop variants) and "lenient" (wider thresholds, prioritize availability/cost).

Decision tree sketch

We want a compact decision tree that operators can read off quickly during incidents. Below is an ASCII sketch mapping the primitive checks into a triage flow:

Request arrival -> Check route override? -> if yes: apply override -> else -> Check local-region health (p95, errors, capacity)
  if local-region OK -> route local-fast-variant
  else -> Check compatible remote-region within latency budget
    if remote OK and cost_delta acceptable -> route remote-same-variant
    else -> Check quantized variants (lower-cost / lower-memory)
      if quantized OK -> route quantized
      else -> Check hosted fallback (SLA allow) -> route hosted-fallback or reject

Decision reasons returned with request metadata: ["local-p95-fail", "remote-capacity-ok", "quantized-succeeds", "hosted-fallback-activated"]

Cost vs latency examples (concrete numbers for toy workloads)

- Baseline: local p95 = 18 ms, cost = $0.0025 / request, capacity_util = 0.6
- Remote region A: p95 = 38 ms, cost = $0.0030 / request
- Quantized variant: p95 = 45 ms, cost = $0.0017 / request, quality delta ~ +2% hallucination risk for this workload

Policy example to encode business intent "minimize user-visible latency unless cost delta > $0.0008 or reliability drops":
- Prefer local variant if p95 < 25 and error_rate_1m < 0.5 and cost_delta < 0.0008
- Else prefer remote region if p95 < 50 and error_rate_1m < 1.0 and cost_delta < 0.0012
- Else prefer quantized variant if p95 < 60 and quality_budget_ok
- Else route to hosted with notification

Quality budget and safe-fallbacks

- Introduce a "quality_budget" counter per-tenant: decremented when we select a lower-quality variant. Reset on daily/weekly cadence. This enforces bounded degradation.
- For top-tier tenants, quality_budget thresholds are higher (allow fewer degradations).

Operationalization notes

- Control-plane must snapshot metrics at evaluation time and include staleness TTL (e.g., only accept metrics < 10s old for latency checks).
- Implement a lightweight policy expression evaluator (no JS/WASM). A policy compiler will convert rule blocks into an optimized sequence of predicates and a compact decision table.
- Emit metrics per-rule: evaluation_count, match_count, average_reason_latency. Useful for deciding adjustments.
- Provide a dry-run mode where decisions are computed but not applied; record what would have happened for A/B analysis.

Canary testing plan

1) Start with single-route canary for an internal sandbox tenant. Baseline traffic magnitude ~ 5 RPS.
2) Run dry-run for 24 hours capturing decisions and delta in latency/cost.
3) Flip on apply mode for 1 hour under on-call watch and abort criteria.
4) Gradually increase to customer-like load, track quality regressions (automated evals) and SLO violations.

Edge cases and unresolved questions

- How to incorporate cold-start penalties for auto-scaled pools? (capacity_utilization alone doesn't capture spin-up latency). Possible: include "cold_start_risk" signal from ortho autoscaler.
- Should we add a hysteresis timer to prevent route-churning when metrics hover around threshold? (Yes: implement per-route cooldown, configurable).
- How to represent compound cost calculations for multi-hop decisions (e.g., remote region + egress + model-variant cost)? Need a cost-estimator subcomponent in control plane.
- Per-customer overrides: limit expressivity so support teams can reason about policies (no Turing-complete DSL).

Open experiments to run

- Param sweep for p95 thresholds: run policy with p95 cutoffs at {20,25,30,40} and measure user-latency percentiles and cost delta.
- Quality_budget policy: compare daily reset vs weekly reset and track cumulative quality loss and customer complaints for sandbox tenants.
- Hysteresis durations: 30s vs 2m vs 10m and observe route stability.

Action items (short term)

- [ ] Implement policy expression evaluator prototype (engineering, PR open: orchestrator/#512) - owner: Lin Zhao - ETA: 2026-01-15
- [ ] Add metric-staleness guard to control-plane snapshotting - owner: Rohan - ETA: 2025-09-30
- [ ] Create canary plan and schedule dry-run (internal sandbox) - owner: Ava - ETA: 2025-10-10
- [ ] Create observability dashboard for rule-level metrics - owner: SRE - ETA: 2025-11-05

Notes to self

- Keep rule ordering readable; prefer multiple short rules to one monolithic score function.
- Document decision reasons in the request trace so downstream teams can map user tickets to policy decisions.
- When in doubt, prefer reliability over marginal cost wins for high-SLA customers.

References / links

- See confluence:PLAT-4321 for long-form design doc (draft)
- Jira JIRA-1284: policy engine perf workstream
- Orchestrator PR 512: initial evaluator prototype

End of notes.
